title: The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and Peter's Denial
summary: As Passover approaches, Judas agrees to hand Jesus over to the chief priests. At the Passover meal Jesus gives his disciples bread and cup as his body given for them and the new covenant in his blood, then teaches them that the greatest must be like one who serves, promises them a kingdom, and warns Peter that he will deny him. On the Mount of Olives he prays in anguish, is arrested after Judas's kiss, and is taken to the high priest's house, where Peter three times denies knowing him. At daybreak the council questions him, and he speaks of the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God.
story:
Luke's account of the passion, the suffering and death of Jesus, begins here. Since 9:51 Jesus has been walking resolutely toward Jerusalem, and since his arrival (19:45-21:38) he has taught daily in the temple while the leaders looked for a way to kill him without provoking the crowd (19:47-48, 20:19, 21:37-38). They find it through one of the Twelve. At the Passover, the feast that remembered Israel's rescue from Egypt, Jesus gives the meal a new center: himself, given for them, and a new covenant sealed in his blood.

The chapter moves from table to garden to courtyard to council, and at every stage the disciples fail while Jesus stays faithful. They argue about rank at the table, sleep while he prays, reach for swords when he is arrested, and Peter, their spokesman, denies him three times. Satan, who left Jesus after the testing in the wilderness until an opportune time (4:13), now returns, entering Judas (verse 3) and asking to sift the disciples like wheat (verse 31). Yet Jesus has already prayed for Peter, and he gives him a task for after his return: strengthen your brothers. Acts shows Peter doing exactly that (Acts 1:15, 2:14). The chapter ends with Jesus before the council of Israel's leaders, making the claim on which the rest of the story turns: from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God. Chapter 23 takes him to Pilate, to Herod, and to the cross.
historical:
Passover (Hebrew pesach, Greek pascha) remembered the exodus (Exodus 12). The lambs were slaughtered in the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, in March or April, and eaten that night, which by Jewish reckoning had already become 15 Nisan; the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread followed (Leviticus 23:5-8), and by the first century the two names covered the whole festival, as Luke's opening words show (verse 1). Josephus uses the same combined language (Antiquities 14.21, 17.213). Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims, and every lamb had to be eaten within the city, which is why Jesus asks for a room inside the walls (verses 10-12). Luke, like Mark and Matthew, presents the Last Supper as a Passover meal (verses 7-8, 15), while John appears to place Jesus' death on the afternoon the lambs were killed (John 18:28, 19:14). The main explanations, a different calendar, a Passover meal held a day early, or John's theological timing, are set out in the notes on Mark 14. The crucifixion is most often dated to AD 30 or 33, the years in which 14 or 15 Nisan fell on a Friday within the terms of Pilate (about AD 26 to 36) and Caiaphas (about AD 18 to 36 or 37).

Luke names the high priest in his preface to John's ministry, in the time of Annas and Caiaphas (3:2), and in Acts calls Annas ‘the high priest’ with Caiaphas beside him (Acts 4:6). Annas had held the office from about AD 6 to 15, and five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held it after him (Josephus, Antiquities 18.26, 18.34-35, 20.197-198), so the title stayed with him. In 1990 an ornate ossuary inscribed with the name Joseph son of Caiaphas was found in a family tomb in south Jerusalem. Luke alone speaks of stratēgoi, officers of the temple (verses 4 and 52). In Acts the captain of the temple arrests Peter and John (Acts 4:1, 5:24-26), and Josephus mentions the same officer (Jewish War 6.294). They commanded the Levitical temple police, which explains the swords and clubs of the arresting party (verse 52).

The council (sunedrion, verse 66, from which the Hebrew Sanhedrin is borrowed) was the ruling body of chief priests, elders, and scribes, with the high priest presiding. Luke's account differs from Mark's here. Mark and Matthew describe a night hearing with false witnesses and the charge that Jesus threatened the temple; Luke has only mockery in the night (verses 63-65) and a single session at daybreak (verse 66), with no witnesses and no temple charge, which he reserves for the trial of Stephen (Acts 6:13-14). Many historians find a morning session more plausible, since the Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, forbids capital trials at night (m. Sanhedrin 4:1), though whether its rules reflect Sadducean practice in the 30s is disputed (see Mark 14). According to John 18:31, the council could not carry out a death sentence itself, and the Jerusalem Talmud remembers that the right to try capital cases was taken away forty years before the temple fell (y. Sanhedrin 1:1). Stephen's stoning (Acts 7) and the execution of James, the brother of Jesus, during a gap between governors in AD 62 (Antiquities 20.200-203), for which the high priest Ananus was deposed, look like irregular exceptions. So the case had to go to Pilate.
cultural:
At the Passover meal free people reclined on couches or cushions, leaning on the left elbow, and the Mishnah requires even the poorest Israelite to recline that night (m. Pesachim 10:1). The meal followed an order that the Mishnah describes in its developed form (m. Pesachim 10): four cups of wine, unleavened bread, bitter herbs, a dish for dipping, the lamb, a son's questions and the father's retelling of the exodus, and the singing of the Hallel psalms (113-118). The third cup was drunk after the meal with the grace after eating (m. Pesachim 10:7), which is why many identify the cup ‘after supper’ (verse 20; compare 1 Corinthians 11:25) with it and with Paul's ‘cup of blessing’ (1 Corinthians 10:16). How much of that order was fixed in Jesus' day is debated, but Luke's two cups, one before the bread (verses 17-18) and one after the meal (verse 20), fit a meal with several cups, and the host's act of interpreting the food is exactly what Jesus does. A man carrying a water jar (verse 10) would have been easy to spot, since fetching water was usually women's work, and householders in Jerusalem made guest rooms available to pilgrims; the word for guest room, kataluma, is the one Luke used at Jesus' birth (2:7).

In verse 25 Jesus names the social order of the Greek and Roman world. Kings took the title Benefactor (euergetēs), as Ptolemy III Euergetes of Egypt did in the third century BC, and cities put up inscriptions honoring patrons as benefactors in return for gifts, which bound the recipients in obligation and loyalty. Jesus does not deny that leaders exist; he reverses the flow of honor. The youngest (verse 26) had the lowest status at table, and in a household the one who served stood while the master reclined (compare 17:7-8). Jesus places himself in the servant's position (verse 27), which John illustrates with the washing of feet at the same meal (John 13:1-17).

The swords of verse 38 were machairai, short swords or long knives that travelers carried against bandits. Josephus says that even the Essenes, who carried nothing else on a trip, took weapons because of robbers (Jewish War 2.125), and the road from Jericho to Jerusalem was notorious for them (10:30). A disciple greeted his teacher with a kiss, which made Judas's signal both inconspicuous and bitter (verse 48). Jews usually prayed standing (18:11, 18:13), so Jesus' kneeling (verse 41) marks intensity, as with Solomon at the temple's dedication (1 Kings 8:54) and later Stephen and Paul (Acts 7:60, 20:36). Jerusalem stands about 750 meters (some 2,500 feet) above sea level, and spring nights are cold, which is why a fire burned in the courtyard (verse 55). Peter's Galilean origin was recognizable (verse 59), by his accent according to Matthew 26:73. The blindfold game of verse 64 made a sport of Jesus' reputation as a prophet at the very moment his prophecy about Peter was coming true in the courtyard.
literary:
The chapter has three movements: the supper (verses 1-38), the Mount of Olives (39-53), and the night and morning at the high priest's house (54-71). At the table Luke sets a farewell discourse, a well-known ancient form in which a leader facing death gives final teaching, warnings, and promises: Jacob's blessing of his sons (Genesis 49), Moses' last words (Deuteronomy 33), the Jewish Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, Jesus' long discourse in John 13-17, and Paul's farewell at Miletus, which Luke himself records (Acts 20:17-38). Only Luke places the dispute about greatness at the Last Supper (Mark sets a similar exchange on the road, Mark 10:42-45), only Luke sets at the supper the promise of a table and thrones in the kingdom (verses 28-30; Matthew 19:28 has the thrones in another setting), and only Luke has the prayer for Peter (31-32), and the saying about purse, bag, and sword (35-38).

Contrast drives the whole chapter: Jesus serves while the disciples argue about rank; Jesus prays while they sleep; Jesus heals the man his follower has wounded (verse 51, only in Luke); Jesus confesses before the council while Peter denies him in the courtyard. Luke tells the Mount of Olives scene more briefly than Mark, with one prayer rather than three and the disciples sleeping ‘from sorrow’ (verse 45), a kinder explanation. The frame of the scene, pray that you will not enter into temptation (verses 40 and 46), shows what Jesus is teaching by example. Bart Ehrman and Mark Plunkett (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1983) argued that without verses 43-44 the passage forms a neat chiasm centered on the prayer of verse 42, one of their reasons for thinking those verses were added (see the text note).

Luke's order in verses 54-71 differs from Mark's: the denial comes first, then the mockery, then the hearing at daybreak. The effect is to set Peter's failure and Jesus' faithfulness side by side at the same hour, joined by one detail found only in Luke: ‘And the Lord turned and looked at Peter’ (verse 61). The time words mark the passion as the hour Jesus had spoken of: ‘when the hour had come’ (verse 14), and ‘this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness’ (verse 53). Luke's key word for God's plan, dei, ‘it is necessary’, appears in verse 37: what is written about Jesus ‘must be fulfilled’, and he cites Isaiah 53:12, the only place in the Gospels where Jesus explicitly quotes the fourth Servant Song. Many details anticipate Acts, where Peter strengthens his brothers, the Twelve face a dispute about serving tables (Acts 6:1-4), and Stephen stands before the same council.

outline.t: Judas agrees to betray Jesus
Preparing the Passover
The Last Supper and the new covenant

doctrines.note: The Lord's Supper is instituted here with the command “do this in remembrance of Me” (verse 19), words that appear in the Gospels only in Luke and in Paul's account (1 Corinthians 11:24-25). Christians agree the Supper is central to the church's worship and differ on how Christ is present in it: Roman Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that the bread and wine become his body and blood, Lutherans that he is truly present in, with, and under them, Reformed Christians that he is spiritually present and received by faith, and many Baptists and others that it is chiefly a memorial and proclamation. Each reads these verses carefully in support of its view.

“This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (verse 20) joins two Old Testament texts: the blood of the covenant Moses sprinkled at Sinai (Exodus 24:8) and the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31:31-34, in which God will write his law on hearts and remember sins no more. Jesus presents his death as the act that brings that promised covenant into being.

Jesus interprets his coming death as his body “given for you” and his blood “poured out for you” (verses 19-20), the language of sacrifice given on behalf of others. He also applies Isaiah 53:12 to himself: the Servant who is counted among the transgressors is the one who bears the sin of many. His death is neither an accident nor a defeat but what was written and determined (verses 22, 37).

Jesus refuses the model of the Gentile kings who lord it over others and call themselves benefactors (verse 25). Leaders among his people are to be like the youngest and the servant, because he himself is among them as one who serves (verses 26-27). The kingdom he confers (verse 29) is exercised on that pattern, which Acts shows the apostles learning (Acts 6:1-4).

Jesus prays for Peter before Peter falls (verse 32), and in the garden he prays honestly that the cup might pass while submitting to the Father's will: “Yet not My will, but Yours be done” (verse 42). He twice tells the disciples to pray so as not to enter into temptation (verses 40, 46). Prayer is the way Jesus faces the hour of darkness, and the way he teaches his followers to face theirs.

words.note: Diathēkē, covenant. It occurs 33 times in the New Testament, 17 of them in Hebrews and only twice in Luke: the covenant with Abraham (1:72) and the new covenant here (verse 20). In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew berit, the binding relationship God makes with his people, with promises and obligations. In ordinary Greek it could mean a will or testament, a sense Hebrews 9:16-17 plays on, but the standard lexicons agree that biblical usage is governed by the Hebrew idea of a covenant God himself establishes.

Anamnēsis, remembrance, a reminder. It occurs only four times in the New Testament: here (verse 19), twice in Paul's account of the Supper (1 Corinthians 11:24-25), and in Hebrews 10:3 of the annual reminder of sins in the old sacrifices. In the Septuagint the related language describes memorials before God (Leviticus 24:7, Numbers 10:10). Biblical remembering is more than recalling a fact: Passover made the exodus present to every generation (Exodus 12:14, 13:8). Christians differ on how far to press the word, whether toward a memorial made before God, a making present of the one sacrifice, or a thankful recollection by the church, but all agree the Supper remembers Christ's death.

Paradidōmi, to hand over, deliver up. It occurs 119 times in the New Testament and 17 in Luke, six of them in this chapter and the next (22:4, 6, 21, 22, 48; 23:25). It is the verb of the passion predictions: the Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men (9:44, 18:32, 24:7). It does not by itself mean ‘betray’; context supplies the treachery. The same verb describes Judas handing Jesus to the priests, the priests handing him to Pilate (24:20), Pilate handing him over to their will (23:25), and, in Paul, God giving up his Son for us all (Romans 8:32) and the Son giving himself (Galatians 2:20).

Diakoneō, to serve, originally to wait on tables. It occurs 37 times in the New Testament, eight in Luke, three of them in verses 26-27. Luke uses it of Peter's mother-in-law (4:39), of the women who supported Jesus from their means (8:3), of Martha (10:40), and of the master who will astonishingly serve his watchful servants (12:37). “But I am among you as one who serves” (verse 27) makes table service the shape of Jesus' own life, and the related noun gives the church the word deacon (Acts 6:1-2).

Peirasmos, testing or temptation. It occurs 21 times in the New Testament, six in Luke. The word covers both a trial that proves faith and an enticement to sin, and the Lord's Prayer asks not to be led into it (11:4). Luke uses it for the devil's testing of Jesus (4:13), for the time of testing in which shallow believers fall away (8:13), for the trials in which the disciples stood by Jesus (verse 28), and for the danger he twice tells them to pray against in the garden (verses 40, 46). Sleep leaves them unready for the trial that comes within the hour.

Agōnia, anguish, agony, in Greek usage the tension and distress of a contestant before a struggle (agōn). It occurs only here in the New Testament (verse 44), together with hidrōs, sweat, and thromboi, clots or drops, also found nowhere else. The comparison is a simile (hōsei, ‘like’): Luke says the sweat was like drops of blood falling to the ground, and interpreters differ on whether he means blood-tinged sweat or sweat falling as heavily as blood. The verse's place in the text is itself uncertain (see the text note).

Lēstēs, robber, bandit, and in Josephus often an armed rebel against Rome (Jewish War 2.253-254). It occurs 15 times in the New Testament, four in Luke: the robbers on the Jericho road (10:30, 10:36), the ‘den of robbers’ Jesus says the temple has become (19:46), and his protest at the arrest, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as you would against an outlaw?” (verse 52). Barabbas is called a lēstēs in John 18:40, and Mark calls the men crucified with Jesus lēstai (Mark 15:27). The man arrested as an outlaw will die among outlaws, as verse 37 said.

christ:
The chapter shows what kind of Messiah Jesus is. He is the host of Israel's Passover who gives himself as its meaning: the bread is his body given for them, and the cup the new covenant in his blood. Passover remembered the lamb whose blood protected Israel on the night of the exodus (Exodus 12:13), and Paul could later write that Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). Luke does not use that phrase, but he sets Jesus' words about his body and blood at the Passover table, on the day the lambs were sacrificed (verse 7), and joins them to the covenant blood of Sinai (Exodus 24:8) and the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34. He also looks forward: he will not eat the Passover again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God (verse 16), and he appoints to his disciples a kingdom in which they will eat and drink at his table (verse 30). The Supper stands between the exodus and the messianic banquet the prophets foresaw (Isaiah 25:6-8).

He is the Servant. He is among his disciples as one who serves (verse 27), and he names himself as the one of whom Isaiah wrote that he was numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12, verse 37). The same Servant Song says he bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors, and in this chapter Jesus intercedes for Peter before the fall (verse 32) and heals the servant of the high priest after the blow (verse 51). On the Mount of Olives he is the obedient Son. His prayer, “Yet not My will, but Yours be done” (verse 42), is the Lord's Prayer lived out under the greatest pressure (11:2), and it shows both the real human will of the Son and its perfect submission to the Father, a point the church later made central in its confession of Christ's two natures (see the interpretation note).

Before the council he answers as the Son of Man of Daniel 7:13-14, who receives an everlasting kingdom, and as the Lord of Psalm 110:1, invited to sit at God's right hand. Luke's wording, “from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God” (verse 69), omits Mark's reference to coming with the clouds and stresses that the enthronement begins now, with the passion, a claim Acts announces at Pentecost (Acts 2:33-36) and Stephen sees fulfilled (Acts 7:56). His answer to the question whether he is the Son of God, ‘You say that I am’ (verse 70), neither denies the title nor claims it on their terms, and they take it as a confession. The one on trial is the true judge, and his steadfastness stands against the failure of every disciple, including Peter, for whom he has already prayed. The look he gives Peter (verse 61) is the look of the Lord who knew the denial was coming and had already provided for the return.
interpretation:
The words over the bread and cup are the most interpreted lines in the chapter, and their reception begins in the New Testament. Luke's longer text is close to Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, written around AD 54, which shares the phrases ‘given for you’, ‘do this in remembrance of me’, ‘after supper’, and ‘the new covenant in my blood’. The Didache (9-10, around AD 100) gives prayers of thanksgiving over cup and bread in that order, and Justin Martyr (First Apology 66, around 155) quotes the command to do this in remembrance. Justin also cites the sweat like drops of blood from what he calls the memoirs of the apostles (Dialogue with Trypho 103), and Irenaeus uses it against those who denied that Christ had a real body (Against Heresies 3.22.2). In the fourth century the same verses became a weapon in the debate over Christ's divinity; Epiphanius reports that some orthodox copyists removed them because they feared that a Son strengthened by an angel looked inferior (Ancoratus 31), and Hilary of Poitiers answered that the Creator of angels did not need the support of creatures (On the Trinity 10.41). In the seventh-century controversy over whether Christ had one will or two, Maximus the Confessor made the Gethsemane prayer his central text for a true human will freely surrendered to the divine, and the Third Council of Constantinople (681) adopted that teaching.

Medieval and Reformation readings divided along the church's larger debates. The Council of Trent taught that by saying ‘Do this in remembrance of me’ Christ instituted the apostles as priests (Session 22, canon 2, 1562), a reading Protestant churches rejected. Pope Boniface VIII's bull Unam Sanctam (1302) read the two swords of verse 38 as the spiritual and temporal powers, both belonging to the church, one wielded by it and one for it. The First Vatican Council's constitution Pastor Aeternus (1870) cited Jesus' prayer that Peter's faith would not fail (verse 32) in defining the infallibility of the pope, while Protestant commentators have read it as a prayer for Peter's own restoration after his denial, the pattern of Christ's intercession for all his people (Romans 8:34, Hebrews 7:25). Theologians and novelists have returned to Judas again and again. Karl Barth devoted a long section of Church Dogmatics II/2 (1942) to him as the test case of election; Jorge Luis Borges's story Three Versions of Judas (1944) imagines a scholar who makes him the true redeemer; William Klassen (Judas: Betrayer or Friend of Jesus?, 1996) argued that the verb paradidōmi means ‘hand over’ and that the earliest tradition did not make him a traitor; and the Gnostic Gospel of Judas, published in 2006, presents him as the disciple who understood Jesus.

Modern critical study has concentrated on Luke's sources and text. Joachim Jeremias (The Eucharistic Words of Jesus) defended the longer text of verses 19-20 and the Passover setting; Bart Ehrman (The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture, 1993) argued for the shorter text. S. G. F. Brandon (Jesus and the Zealots, 1967) cited the sword saying as evidence of revolutionary sympathy, and Martin Hengel answered him (Was Jesus a Revolutionist?, English 1971).

The chapter is at the heart of Holy Week. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year C, Luke 22:14-23:56 is the Passion Gospel for Palm Sunday; in the older Roman rite Luke's passion was sung on the Wednesday of Holy Week. El Greco painted the Agony in the Garden with Luke's angel bearing a cup (Toledo Museum of Art, about 1590 to 1595), and Rembrandt's Denial of Saint Peter (1660, Rijksmuseum) shows Christ, bound in the background, turning to look at Peter as he denies him, a detail only Luke records.
text:
English Bibles differ at two important places in this chapter, both matters of manuscripts rather than translation.

The first is the Supper (verses 17-20). Almost every Greek manuscript has the longer text, in which a cup (17-18) is followed by the bread with the words ‘given for you; do this in remembrance of Me’ (19) and a second cup after supper (20). Codex Bezae (D, fifth century) and several Old Latin manuscripts stop at ‘This is My body’ in verse 19 and lack the rest of 19 and all of 20, leaving one cup before the bread. Other early translations show attempts to smooth the sequence: two Old Latin manuscripts move the bread before the first cup, and the Curetonian and Sinaitic Syriac rearrange the verses in different ways, with the Sinaitic adding words from verse 20. Westcott and Hort (1881) printed the shorter text, treating the longer as one of their ‘Western non-interpolations’ (see the text note on chapter 24), and the Revised Standard Version of 1946 and 1952 followed them; the RSV's second edition (1971) restored the verses. Joachim Jeremias argued that the external evidence overwhelmingly favors the longer text and that some copyists shortened a liturgical formula well known to believers; Bart Ehrman argued that scribes added it to strengthen the teaching that Jesus' death atones. Almost all modern editions and translations print the longer text, often without a note.

The second is the angel and the sweat like drops of blood (verses 43-44). The verses are absent from P75 (around AD 200), Codex Vaticanus (B), Codex Alexandrinus (A), Codex Washingtonianus (W), a corrector of Sinaiticus, probably P69, and some Syriac and Coptic witnesses. They are present in the first hand of Sinaiticus, in Bezae, in 0171 (around 300), and in most later manuscripts, and they were known in the second century to Justin and Irenaeus. Manuscripts of family 13 and several lectionaries place them after Matthew 26:39, a sign of their use in the Holy Week readings. Bart Ehrman and Mark Plunkett (1983) argued that they were added to counter teachers who denied Christ's real humanity; Lincoln Blumell (TC: A Journal of Biblical Textual Criticism, 2014) argued that they were removed, as Epiphanius says some did, because they seemed to diminish Christ. The UBS and Nestle-Aland editions print them in double brackets, and most English Bibles print them with a note. In verse 68 the King James Version adds ‘nor let me go’, following later manuscripts that the earliest lack.

teach.big: At the Passover table and in the hour of darkness Jesus gives himself for his failing disciples, serving them, praying for them, and submitting to the Father's will, and so he establishes the new covenant and the pattern of servant greatness.

outline.t: Human scheming and Satan's work converge on one of the Twelve: nearness to Jesus is no protection without faithfulness.
Jesus is not a victim caught by surprise; he arranges the Passover he will interpret by his death.
Jesus gives his body and blood for his people and establishes the new covenant, and the church keeps this meal in remembrance of him.
God's plan does not excuse the betrayer; the Son goes as it was determined, and woe to the one who hands him over.
In the kingdom greatness is measured by service, because the King himself serves at the table.
Jesus prays for us before we fall, and our failure need not be the end of our usefulness.
The mission now meets hostility, and the Servant must be counted among the lawless; misunderstood swords are no program for the kingdom.
Jesus faces the cup with honest anguish and full surrender, and teaches us to meet temptation with prayer.
Betrayed with a kiss, Jesus rejects violence, heals his enemy, and names the hour of darkness for what it is.
Peter's denial and bitter tears show both the weakness of the best disciple and the look of the Lord who knew and still loved him.
Mocked as a false prophet, Jesus speaks the truth before Israel's council: the Son of Man is about to be seated at God's right hand.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first turns the Supper into a battleground and neglects the text. Each tradition should teach its own understanding of Christ's presence, but not in a way that suggests the other traditions ignore these words; Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, and Baptist Christians all read them carefully. The second preaches the two swords (verses 36-38) either as a charter for Christian armed self-defense or as a medieval proof of church power over the state. The reply ‘That is enough’ and Jesus' rebuke in verse 51 make both uses very hard to sustain.

A third error treats the sweat like drops of blood as a medical fact to be explained in detail. Luke's wording is a comparison, the verses are textually uncertain, and preaching should rest its weight on the prayer of verse 42, which no manuscript lacks. A fourth makes Judas a pure villain unlike ourselves, or, in reaction, a misunderstood hero; Luke holds together Satan's entry, Judas's free choice, God's determined plan, and a real woe. A fifth hurries past Peter's failure to reach the restoration. Luke lets him weep bitterly (verse 62) before any word of comfort, and the look of the Lord is both exposure and mercy. Finally, avoid reading the council scene as a picture of Jewish people in general; the chief priests and elders are a small ruling group, and many in Jerusalem are about to mourn Jesus (23:27, 23:48).
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on people who have been betrayed by someone close, sometimes by a friend or spouse who kept up appearances to the end; Judas's kiss names that wound, and Jesus' own experience of it can be a real comfort. It will also press on those who have failed badly and fear they are finished. Peter's story shows that Jesus knew beforehand, prayed beforehand, and had a task waiting afterward, but teach it without making light of the tears. People in anguish, facing surgery, loss, or a decision that will cost them, can learn from Jesus that honest pleading and surrender belong in the same prayer. And for those who have experienced leaders who dominate and call it service, verses 24-27 are a clear word that Jesus condemns lordship dressed up as benefaction.

hard.q: Why does Jesus tell his disciples to buy swords, and then say two swords are enough?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real. Earlier Jesus sent his disciples out with nothing and told them to turn the other cheek (6:29, 10:4), and a few verses later he stops the use of a sword and heals the wounded man (verses 49-51). Yet here he says the one without a sword should sell his cloak and buy one (verse 36). S. G. F. Brandon (Jesus and the Zealots, 1967) took the saying as evidence that Jesus and his followers were closer to the armed resistance against Rome than the Gospels admit, and that the evangelists softened the picture. Some Christian readers have taken it the other way, as permission for armed self-defense, and medieval popes, above all Boniface VIII in Unam Sanctam (1302), read the two swords as the spiritual and temporal powers entrusted to the church.

Most commentators read the saying differently. Martin Hengel (Was Jesus a Revolutionist?, English 1971) and others answered Brandon that the teaching of Jesus as a whole rules out a program of violence, and that two swords among twelve men would be absurd equipment for a revolt. The majority reading takes verse 36 as vivid, figurative language: the time of welcome on the road is over, and the disciples must be ready for a world as hostile to them as to their master. They take him literally and produce two swords, and his reply, ‘That is enough’ (hikanon estin), is read as a weary closing of a misunderstood conversation, much as one might say ‘enough of that’, rather than an inventory. A second reading, which Luke's own wording supports, ties the swords to verse 37: the Servant must be counted among the lawless, and a band carrying weapons makes the arresting party's charge plausible (verse 52). A third, held by some who defend self-defense, holds that the swords are meant for protection on the road, as travelers commonly carried them, but not for defending Jesus or advancing the kingdom. Justin Meggitt (Journal for the Study of the New Testament, 2023) has recently argued that the disciples' being armed is historical and that Luke's appeal to Isaiah 53:12 explains an awkward memory. All these readings agree that the passage cannot be a charter for violence in Jesus' name, which his own action at the arrest excludes, and Christians still differ, as pacifists and just-war theorists, over what it implies for the use of force in other settings.

hard.q: If Satan entered Judas and the Son of Man went ‘as it has been determined’, how can Judas be blamed?
hard.a:
The objection is ancient and sharp. Verse 3 says Satan entered Judas, verse 22 says the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, and Acts says Jesus was handed over by God's set plan and foreknowledge (Acts 2:23). If the betrayal was planned by God and carried out under Satan's control, a skeptic asks, where is Judas's guilt? Some modern readers have pressed the point sympathetically. William Klassen (Judas: Betrayer or Friend of Jesus?, 1996) argued that paradidōmi simply means ‘hand over’ and that the earliest tradition did not treat Judas as a traitor at all, the demonizing growing in later retellings, and Jorge Luis Borges's story Three Versions of Judas (1944) turned the paradox into a meditation on a redeemer who damned himself. The Gospel of Judas, known to Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.31.1) and published in 2006, went further and made him the one disciple who understood Jesus.

Luke's own answer is to hold the claims together without dissolving them. Judas goes to the chief priests himself (verse 4), bargains, consents, and looks for an opportunity (verses 5-6); the money and the kiss are his. The same sentence that speaks of God's determination pronounces woe on the man who betrays (verse 22), just as Peter will say in Acts that lawless men crucified Jesus and that it happened by God's plan (Acts 2:23). Augustine and Thomas Aquinas spoke of God permitting evil and ordering it to good; Calvin, who distrusted the language of bare permission (Institutes 1.18), insisted that God's purpose and the human intent differ even within a single act, so that the same event can be God's saving plan and a man's betrayal. Arminian and Wesleyan readers stress God's foreknowledge of a free choice rather than a decree, and many Catholic and Orthodox theologians speak of God's providence working through freely chosen evil. Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics II/2) read Judas as the sharpest case of the rejected one for whom Christ was rejected, and left open his final destiny. These are second-order debates about providence and freedom, and Christians remain divided on them. What Luke's text will not allow is either a Judas without responsibility or a plan of God defeated by his betrayal.

observe: What does Jesus say over the bread and over the cup (verses 19-20), and what does he tell the disciples to do?
What are the disciples arguing about at the table, and what example does Jesus give in reply (verses 24-27)?
What detail about Peter's denial does verse 61 add, and what does Peter do next?
interpret: Why do you think Luke places the argument about greatness at the Last Supper, right after Jesus speaks of his body given for them?
What does Jesus' prayer in verse 42 reveal about his relationship with the Father and about the cost of the cross?
How does Luke hold together God's plan and Judas's guilt in verses 3-6 and 22?
apply: Jesus said, ‘I am among you as one who serves.’ Where are you tempted to measure your importance by position rather than service?
Jesus prayed for Peter before he fell and gave him a task for afterward. What does that say to you about a failure you carry?
What would it look like for you to pray both honestly and obediently about something you dread?
